CDFχ2(ΔχMAP2| 2dof)=12​π∫−NNe−t2/2dt,\mathrm{CDF}_{\chi^{2}}\left(\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}}|\,2\,\mathrm{dof}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-N}^{N}e^{-t^{2}/2}dt~, (22)

where the left hand side denotes the cumulative distribution of χ2\chi^{2}. We also compute the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) [144, 145, 146, 147], which takes into account the Bayesian complexity of the model and penalizes including extra parameters.

VII.1 Results

From DESI DR2 BAO alone, we obtain rather weak constraints on the parameters

w0=−0.48−0.17+0.35wa<−1.34}DESI BAO,\left.\begin{aligned} w_{0}&=-0.48^{+0.35}_{-0.17}\\ w_{a}&<-1.34\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{56.9055pt}{\begin{flushleft}DESI BAO, \end{flushleft}}}} (23)

which mildly favor the w0>−1w_{0}>-1, wa<0w_{a}<0 quadrant. The upper bound on waw_{a} here is the 68% limit, and wa=0w_{a}=0 is not excluded at 95%. As was the case in DR1, BAO data alone define a degeneracy direction in the w0w_{0}-waw_{a} plane, but they do not show a strong preference for dark energy evolution: the improvement in χMAP2\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} relative to the Λ\LambdaCDM case of w0=−1w_{0}=-1, wa=0w_{a}=0 is equivalent to a preference of just 1.7σ\sigma. Note that the posteriors in this poorly constrained case are cut off by the priors, so the marginalized means and limits quoted above are prior-dependent.

The minimal extension we consider, beyond BAO data alone, is to add a high-redshift constraint from the early universe. This can be achieved by imposing CMB-derived priors on θ∗\theta_{\ast}, ωb\omega_{\mathrm{b}} and ωbc\omega_{\mathrm{bc}}, as described in Section IV. These priors are independent of the late-time dark energy, and also marginalize over contributions such as the late ISW effect and CMB lensing. Therefore, they provide us with an early time physics prior that can help us set the sound horizon and is based solely on early-Universe information. The result from this data combination is

w0=−0.43±0.22wa=−1.72±0.64}DESI+(θ∗,ωb,ωbc)CMB.\left.\begin{aligned} w_{0}&=-0.43\pm 0.22\\ w_{a}&=-1.72\pm 0.64\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{85.35826pt}{\begin{flushleft}DESI+$(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}})_{\rm CMB}$. \end{flushleft}}}} (24)

While this is still bounded by the wa>−3w_{a}>-3 prior at the lower end, the posterior already clearly disfavors Λ\LambdaCDM. The Δ​χMAP2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} value decreases to −8.0-8.0, indicating a preference for an evolving dark energy equation of state at the 2.4σ\sigma level.

Replacing these minimal early-Universe priors with the full CMB information leads to only a small shift in the maginalized posteriors

w0=−0.42±0.21wa=−1.75±0.58}DESI+CMB,\left.\begin{aligned} w_{0}&=-0.42\pm 0.21\\ w_{a}&=-1.75\pm 0.58\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{56.9055pt}{\begin{flushleft}DESI+CMB, \end{flushleft}}}} (25)

showing that most of the information that the CMB provides on w⁡(z)w(z) comes from its role in anchoring early-Universe values of (θ∗,ωb,ωbc)(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}}) and thus limiting the freedom for models to fit the low-redshift data without an evolving dark energy component. Nevertheless, when including the full CMB information the Δ​χMAP2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} decreases to −12.5-12.5, corresponding to a 3.1σ\sigma preference for evolving dark energy. This change in the Δ​χMAP2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} is driven primarily by the inclusion of CMB lensing, the effect of which is (by construction) not captured in the minimal early-Universe priors (see Appendix A for further discussion and a comparison of posteriors with different choices of CMB likelihoods).

SNe data alone provide a complementary degeneracy direction in the w0w_{0}-waw_{a} plane, as they measure w0w_{0} well independently of waw_{a}, which is only weakly constrained. The combination of SNe data with DESI BAO can therefore measure w0w_{0} and waw_{a} without having the posteriors cut off by the prior ranges we assumed. The marginalized posterior results are listed in Table 5 and depend on the choice of SNe dataset, with the significances of the preference for the model over Λ\LambdaCDM ranging from 1.7​σ1.7\sigma to 3.3​σ3.3\sigma as summarized in Table 6.

However, as discussed in [38], the posterior for the combination of DESI BAO and SNe alone allows quite a wide range of posterior values of ωm\omega_{\mathrm{m}} (or, equivalently, ωc\omega_{\mathrm{c}}). CMB information places extremely tight constraints on ωm\omega_{\mathrm{m}} that are largely independent of the late-time background model. Therefore, the full statistical power of the data is achieved through the combination of the BAO, CMB and SNe datasets, giving the maginalized posterior results

w0=−0.838±0.055wa=−0.62−0.19+0.22}DESI+CMB+ Pantheon+,\left.\begin{aligned} w_{0}&=-0.838\pm 0.055\\ w_{a}&=-0.62^{+0.22}_{-0.19}\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{56.9055pt}{\begin{flushleft}DESI+CMB+ Pantheon+, \end{flushleft}}}} (26)

for the combination with the Pantheon+,

w0=−0.667±0.088wa=−1.09−0.27+0.31}DESI+CMB +Union3,\left.\begin{aligned} w_{0}&=-0.667\pm 0.088\\ w_{a}&=-1.09^{+0.31}_{-0.27}\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{56.9055pt}{\begin{flushleft}DESI+CMB +Union3, \end{flushleft}}}} (27)

with Union3, and

w0=−0.752±0.057wa=−0.86−0.20+0.23}DESI+CMB +DESY5,\left.\begin{aligned} w_{0}&=-0.752\pm 0.057\\ w_{a}&=-0.86^{+0.23}_{-0.20}\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{56.9055pt}{\begin{flushleft}DESI+CMB +DESY5, \end{flushleft}}}} (28)

with DESY5. The posteriors in these three cases, along with the DESI+CMB posterior, are shown in Figure 11. The Δ​χMAP2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} values are −10.7-10.7, −17.4-17.4, and −21.0-21.0, corresponding to preferences for the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model over Λ\LambdaCDM at the 2.8​σ2.8\sigma, 3.8​σ3.8\sigma, and 4.2​σ4.2\sigma levels, for combination with Pantheon+, Union3 and DESY5 respectively. These significances have all increased compared to the values reported in [38] based on the DESI DR1 BAO results.

The deviance information criterion (DIC) values for the combination of DESI+CMB with Pantheon+, Union3 and DESY5 SNe are Δ⁡(DIC)≡DICw0​wa−DICΛ​CDM=−6.8\Delta(\mathrm{DIC})\equiv\mathrm{DIC}_{w_{0}w_{a}}-\mathrm{DIC}_{\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}}=-6.8, −13.5-13.5, −17.2-17.2, respectively. These indicate preferences for the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model consistent with those obtained from the Δ​χMAP2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} values above. Again, the changes in the Δ⁡(DIC)\Delta(\mathrm{DIC}) values obtained here with DESI DR2 BAO data compared to the DR1 values reported in [38] show that the preference for w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM has increased with the additional data. Further details on the calculation of DIC values are given in [49].

The pivot redshift zpz_{\mathrm{p}} at which w⁡(z)w(z) in this parametrization is best constrained by the data depends on the particular combination of datasets used. For DESI+CMB, zp=0.53z_{\mathrm{p}}=0.53 and wp=w⁡(zp)=−1.024±0.043w_{\mathrm{p}}=w(z_{\mathrm{p}})=-1.024\pm 0.043: this is a lower pivot redshift and a tighter constraint on wpw_{\mathrm{p}} than that found for the same combination with DR1 BAO in [38], reflecting the additional constraining power of the DR2 BAO results. For the DESI+CMB+DESY5 combination, we find zp=0.31z_{\mathrm{p}}=0.31 and wp=−0.954±0.024w_{\mathrm{p}}=-0.954\pm 0.024, indicating a mild preference for a deviation from w=−1w=-1 at the best-measured redshift. As the other two SNe datasets are slightly less constraining than DESY5, the pivot redshifts for combinations with them are slightly larger, as are the uncertainties on wpw_{\mathrm{p}}, but the results for all choices of DESI+CMB+SNe are mutually consistent.

These results sharpen the preference already seen in [38] for an evolving equation of state for dark energy: although the statistical significances from all data depend somewhat on the choice of SNe dataset included, even the weakest of them (the DESI+CMB+Pantheon+ combination) is still nearly 3​σ3\sigma, and the significance is 3.1​σ3.1\sigma even when excluding all SNe data altogether (DESI+CMB). In all cases, the favored w⁡(z)w(z) shows a phase of w>−1w>-1 at low redshifts and a phantom crossing to w<−1w<-1 above redshifts z≃0.4z\simeq 0.4. Within the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model, the necessity of such a crossing and the redshift at which it occurs is determined by the requirement to match the precise CMB measurement of θ∗\theta_{\ast} together with Ωm\Omega_{m} [148]. The details of the recovered form of w⁡(z)w(z) and the w0w_{0}, waw_{a} parameter values naturally depend on the choice of parametrization. The accompanying paper [49] explores various other parametrizations of w⁡(z)w(z) beyond Eq. 9, and non-parametric reconstruction methods, that exhibit a similar behavior. Reference [49] also performs binned reconstruction of w⁡(z)w(z) without assuming a functional form for the equation of state and finds a consistent picture, as shown in Figure 12. The lowest redshift bin shown in the figure favors a value of w>−1w>-1 at high significance [49], inconsistent with the Λ\LambdaCDM expectation w=−1w=-1.

The apparent preference for phantom crossing to w⁡(z)<−1w(z)<-1 at intermediate redshifts, and the consequent violation of the NEC, is thus rather independent of parametrization choices made in the analysis (see, e.g., [149] using DR1 data for non-parametric results). However, the equation of state is not directly observable, and we only observe quantities, such as distances, that depend indirectly on w⁡(z)w(z). In some circumstances it may therefore be possible to construct particular models that provide reasonable fits to the low-redshift data while still respecting w⁡(z)≥−1w(z)\geq-1 at all zz ([150, 151] provide explicit examples, but [152] discusses the general limitations of such models in fitting DESI+CMB data). The supporting paper [49] examines several NEC-respecting models of dark energy evolution and finds that while they can somewhat outperform Λ\LambdaCDM, they have low Δ⁡(DIC)\Delta(\text{DIC}) values relative to w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM for the combination of DESI, CMB and SNe data, indicating a preference for phantom crossing.

Table 5 gives a more complete list of the results for other parameters when fitting this model to different combinations of data. It is worth noting that allowing w⁡(z)w(z) to vary does not help resolve the so-called Hubble tension [153], since in w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM the recovered H0H_{0} is lower than the Planck Λ\LambdaCDM value. Although not discussed here, [46] showed that allowing evolving dark energy also does not affect the value of the S8S_{8} parameter determined from DESI data, which remains consistent with values from the CMB.

VII.2 The nature of the evidence for evolving dark energy

The Hubble diagrams in Figure 13 illustrate the nature of the evidence for evolving dark energy and its dependence on the adopted datasets. The upper panels show the isotropic, perpendicular, and parallel BAO measurements (αiso\alpha_{\mathrm{iso}}, α⟂\alpha_{\perp}, and α|⁣|\alpha_{||}), which are normalized to the predictions of the Planck Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology. The lower panels plot μ−μfid\mu-\mu_{\mathrm{fid}}, the distance modulus relative to the fiducial Planck Λ\LambdaCDM prediction, for the three SNe datasets (noting again that for uncalibrated SNe, the distance modulus is only known to an arbitrary constant offset). Our procedure for creating binned data points from the SNe data is described in Section IV.3. Because the fiducial SNe absolute magnitude is unknown, all data points are free to move up or down together by the same amount in μ\mu, and we have chosen the normalization such that error-weighted mean of μ−μfid\mu-\mu_{\mathrm{fid}} is equal to zero. Equivalently, any model curve in these panels can be shifted up or down by a constant Δ​μ\Delta\mu, and we have normalized them to match the weighted mean of the data.

In all panels, the horizontal black line represents the prediction of the Λ\LambdaCDM model best fit by the CMB, with the 1​σ1\sigma range of these predictions shown by the shaded gray region. This differs very slightly from the fiducial cosmology based on the Planck 2018 results, due to the switch from Plik to CamSpec and the addition of ACT lensing data, explaining the slight offset from unity. The blue solid curve shows predictions for the Λ\LambdaCDM model that best fits the DESI BAO data, while purple represents the model fit to DESI+CMB, which closely matches the best fit to DESI with just the (θ∗,ωb,ωbc)(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}}) early-Universe priors from the CMB (see Table 5). The orange curves in each of the lower panels represent the Λ\LambdaCDM models that, from left to right, best fit the DESY5, Union3 and Pantheon+ SNe data respectively. The orange curves in the top row are all those for the Λ\LambdaCDM DESY5 best fit.

While the statistical significance of disagreement cannot be judged accurately from this plot alone, the DESI measurements clearly prefer lower distances (by 1-2%) than the Planck Λ\LambdaCDM prediction at redshifts z≤1z\leq 1. There is a Λ\LambdaCDM model that fits the DESI data well (blue curve), but it has a lower Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} than the Planck model (0.297 vs. 0.317), as shown previously in Figure 8. The joint-fit model (purple curve) has an intermediate Ωm=0.303\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}=0.303, and consequently has a worse fit to both DESI BAO and the CMB (top panels) and also fails to describe the SNe data (lower panels). Similarly, the DESY5 data in the lower left panel exhibit a tension with Planck Λ\LambdaCDM, primarily because of the contrast between the low redshift (z<0.1z<0.1) data at μ−μfid≈0.03\mu-\mu_{\mathrm{fid}}\approx 0.03 and the points at higher redshift. The story is similar for Union3, but for Pantheon+ the value of μ−μfid\mu-\mu_{\mathrm{fid}} at low redshift is smaller, only 0.01.

As is the case for BAO, there exist Λ\LambdaCDM models that can reasonably fit the SNe data (orange curves), but these have large Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} that do not well match CMB constraints and are also strongly inconsistent with DESI data, which prefer an Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} value that is lower than Planck, not higher. Conversely, the conflict with the DESI-constrained Λ\LambdaCDM models (purple and blue curves) and DESY5 SNe is 0.04 in μ\mu at low redshifts, z<0.1z<0.1, which is worse than the 0.03 offset from the Planck fiducial model. All these observations point to the fact that the Λ\LambdaCDM model struggles to consistently fit all three datasets: BAO, CMB, and SNe.

One way to address this tension is to adopt a model with more flexibility in the background expansion. However, the wwCDM model with a constant equation of state lacks sufficient flexibility. The cyan dotted curves in the top row and bottom left show a model with constant w=−0.971w=-0.971 and Ωm=0.310\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}=0.310, which is the wwCDM model that best fits the DESI+CMB+DESY5 data combination; in the remaining two panels the cyan curves show the predictions of very similar models obtained by substituting Union3 or Pantheon+ for DESY5. The high-zz anchor does not allow enough redshift evolution for this model to provide a good fit to the BAO and SNe data at low redshifts, performing only slightly better than Planck Λ\LambdaCDM. If instead the wwCDM model were chosen to fit the DESI+DESY5 data, it would necessarily have an Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} value that would fail to match the CMB constraints on (θ∗,ωb,ωbc)(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}}).

On the other hand, the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model does have sufficient flexibility to simultaneously achieve good fits to all three datasets. The green dashed and red dashed curves in the top panels show predictions for w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM models with parameters matching the best fits to DESI+DESY5 and DESI+CMB+DESY5 respectively. These are barely distinguishable in the plots, showing that the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model that best fits the BAO and SNe automatically also provides a good fit to the CMB. Over the range of redshifts covered by DESI BAO, these model predictions provide a better fit to BAO data than the best such Λ\LambdaCDM model—in particular, in the fit to the parallel BAO distances α|⁣|\alpha_{||}—while also simultaneously resolving the mismatch in Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} between DESI and CMB in the Λ\LambdaCDM framework. The bottom left panel also shows that they are also equally good at fitting the μ\mu offsets between low-zz and high-zz DESY5 data. These observations qualitatively help to explain why these models are strongly preferred over Λ\LambdaCDM.

In the equivalent curves in the center and right panels on the bottom row, DESY5 is replaced in all fits by Union3 and Pantheon+, respectively. While the qualitative picture is the same for Union3 as DESY5, the value of μ−μfid\mu-\mu_{\mathrm{fid}} at low redshift is smaller for Pantheon+ and so using this dataset does not strengthen the preference for evolving dark energy relative to that already provided by the joint fit to DESI and the CMB.

VII.3 Are alternative explanations possible?

Given the surprising results from our analysis—our best-fit evolving dark energy models apparently imply phantom dark energy at some redshifts, and order unity changes in ww over the redshift range spanned by the observations considered—it is worth considering alternative explanations for the data.

The simplest of these alternatives is simply a statistical fluctuation. Based on the Δ​χMAP2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} values presented in Section VII.1 above, the statistical preference for the best-fit w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model over Λ\LambdaCDM ranges from around 3​σ3\sigma to over 4​σ4\sigma, depending on the combination of datasets considered. This level of significance is not trivially dismissed, even if it does not yet rise to the 5​σ5\sigma threshold commonly accepted for establishing new physics. The variations in the statistical significance within this range with the choice of SNe sample also highlight the importance of calibrating the low-to-intermediate redshift SNe distance scale.

The constraining power of SNe in measuring the equation of state comes primarily from the comparison of low-redshift (z<0.1z<0.1) and high redshift (z>0.1z>0.1) supernovae. For supernovae at z>0.1z>0.1, which partially overlap the redshift range of DESI, the Λ\LambdaCDM model that best fits the DESI data is also a good fit to the SNe data. Relative to models that best fit each of the DESY5, Union3 and Pantheon+ SNe samples alone, over the full redshift range, the DESI best-fit model gives only small shifts in the quality of the fit to the SNe data, with Δ​χ2=−1.2\Delta\chi^{2}=-1.2, 1.5 and 2.3 respectively. Unfortunately, no SNe compilation yet exists in which objects from both redshift regimes were collected as part of a uniform observational program. The Pantheon+ and Union3 datasets are compilations of SNe observed in many individual datasets, each with different calibrations and selection functions. Even for the DESY5 dataset, while 1635 SNe with z>0.1z>0.1 come from the DES survey program with homogeneous calibration, 194 SNe at z<0.1z<0.1 are drawn from a mix of historical observational programs with the best-controlled calibrations. The consistent calibration and processing of these data is therefore a delicate operation. Recently, [154] noted an offset in the differences between the standardized brightnesses of low-zz and high-zz SNe for objects in common between the DESY5 and Pantheon+ samples; however, [155] explain the causes for this and argue that the differences are well justified.

If we exclude the low-z sample entirely and take only the DESY5 SNe, which is the most uniformly calibrated sample, naturally the constraining power and thus the statistical significance of the preference for evolution is reduced, but the best-fit values of w0w_{0} and waw_{a} remain far from Λ\LambdaCDM (central panel of Figure 14). Even if SNe at all redshifts are excluded altogether, the statistical significance of the preference from DESI+CMB alone still exceeds 3​σ3\sigma. Future cosmology analyses of homogeneous SNe samples from ZTF [156, 157] and LSST [158, 159] may shed further light on the relative calibration across redshifts.

Using the simple early-Universe prior on (θ∗,ωb,ωbc)(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}}) that marginalizes over information dependent on late-time models in addition to DESI gives very similar posterior constraints on w0w_{0} and waw_{a} to the full DESI+CMB combination (left panel of Figure 14), and the central w0w_{0}, waw_{a} values are very stable. However, the tension with Λ\LambdaCDM drops somewhat (from 3.1σ\sigma to 2.4​σ2.4\sigma) when using these simple priors instead of the full CMB: this is because the (Planck+ACT) CMB lensing likelihood makes a sizable contribution to the Δ​χMAP2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} calculation.

Although recent independent results from SPT [160] and ACT [104] find cosmological parameter values that are consistent with those from Planck, another possibility is that the CMB constraints used here suffer from some unknown systematic error. It is therefore interesting to consider the constraints that can be obtained entirely independent of the high-redshift CMB anchor. As argued in Section VII.2, the primary role of this CMB anchor is that it limits the freedom to vary Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} when fitting to the low-redshift BAO and SNe distance-redshift measurements. This can be achieved instead by replacing the CMB with the DESY3 (3×\times2pt) information to obtain a constraint coming entirely from low-redshift cosmological probes. As shown in the right panel of Figure 14, this combination favors the same region of parameter space, although with somewhat larger uncertainties.

We also consider the possibility of an undetected systematic error in our BAO measurements that would have evaded the many internal checks we have performed (cf. details in [21, 48, 63]). For instance, a coherent systematic shift of 1.5% to all the measured αiso\alpha_{\rm iso} values (Eq. 11), applied in a redshift-independent manner to all tracers, would decrease the tension between DESI and Planck in the Λ\LambdaCDM model, and thus decrease the evidence for evolving dark energy.2020 20 Such a shift would result in the DESI contours in Figure 8 shifting ∼1.5%\sim 1.5\% to the left and thus overlapping the Planck CMB results in Λ\LambdaCDM. However, any such hypothetical shift could not be explained by a simple change in the physical value of rdr_{\mathrm{d}}, as that would also shift the CMB constraints. However, the required magnitude of such a hypothetical shift exceeds the total systematic error budget indicated by our tests by a factor of 6 (for QSO) to 10 (for BGS and LRGs), and we consider this highly unlikely.

Physical models that can satisfactorily explain the data without requiring dark energy evolution are more challenging. Table 5 confirms the finding, previously reported in [38], that allowing the curvature ΩK\Omega_{\mathrm{K}} to vary freely, while increasing uncertainties, does not shift the posterior in w0w_{0} and waw_{a} towards Λ\LambdaCDM. While we have fixed ∑mν=0.06\sum m_{\nu}=0.06 eV for our fiducial analysis, it is allowed to vary in Section VIII below, and we find that this has almost no effect on the dark energy constraints. This is because fitting the CMB power spectrum imposes a positive correlation between ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} and Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}, thus given a physical prior that ∑mν>0\sum m_{\nu}>0 eV, in most of the available parameter space neutrino masses can only increase the CMB value of Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}, which exacerbates rather than relieves the tension with DESI BAO, and in the region where 0≤∑mν≤0.060\leq\sum m_{\nu}\leq 0.06 eV they have very limited effect. However, the more exotic scenario where ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} is treated as an ‘effective’ neutrino mass such that values ∑mν,eff<0\sum m_{\nu,{\rm eff}}<0 eV are allowed [161, 162, 163] can allow CMB fits to be consistent with lower Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}. This has the effect of improving the Λ\LambdaCDM fit and thus reducing the preference for evolving dark energy from DESI+CMB+SNe, but not below the level that is found from the relevant DESI+SNe combination alone without any CMB information (which can be up to 3.3σ\sigma, Table 6), as shown in Section VIII. That is, allowing negative effective neutrino masses still does not fully remove the preference for non-cosmological constant dark energy. At the same time, such dark energy models do permit ∑mν,eff>0\sum m_{\nu,{\rm eff}}>0 values that are consistent with terrestrial experiments. More standard extensions, such as varying the number of effective neutrino species, NeffN_{\mathrm{eff}}, have no effect on the dark energy results.

Arguably, the least contorted way to reconcile our findings with Λ\LambdaCDM is to exclude all constraints from SNe data (on the grounds that the significance depends on the choice of SNe dataset and we have no a priori reason to choose one over the others), and then dismiss the remaining 3.1​σ3.1\sigma discrepancy with DESI+CMB (or 2.7​σ2.7\sigma when also not including CMB lensing) as a statistical fluke.

VIII Neutrinos

Cosmological observations are sensitive to the sum of the neutrino masses. However, this measurement depends on the choice of a cosmological model. So far, our baseline analysis has assumed the sum of neutrino masses to be fixed to the minimum value allowed by terrestrial experiments under a normal mass ordering, ∑mν=0.06\sum m_{\nu}=0.06 eV, modeled as a single massive and two massless states. In this section we allow ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} to vary. When doing so, we assume by default three degenerate mass eigenstates except when testing specific physical mass ordering scenarios. This model produces a good approximation of the observable effects of both normal and inverted physical mass ordering scenarios and, in the case of a positive detection of neutrino masses, would recover the correct ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} value without bias [34, 164]. We also impose a minimal physical (uniform) prior ∑mν>0\sum m_{\nu}>0 eV, while noting that scenarios with negative ‘effective’ neutrino mass have also recently been discussed (e.g., [161, 162, 163]). Supporting paper [50] explores the implications of different modelling assumptions in greater detail.

Primordial neutrinos were copiously produced before the nucleosynthesis era and decoupled at a temperature of about 1​MeV1\,\text{MeV}; see, e.g., [34] for a review of neutrino cosmology. As the Universe expanded, neutrinos gradually lost kinetic energy, behaving as radiation in the early Universe and transitioning to non-relativistic matter around redshifts of z∼100z\sim 100 for realistic neutrino masses, thereafter influencing the late-time expansion history by contributing to the matter component. The main effect of massive neutrinos on the CMB is to impact the angular diameter distance to last scattering, which is degenerate with the effects of other cosmological parameters such as Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} and H0H_{0} (see, e.g., [165] for a recent discussion). Neutrinos also affect the lensing of CMB anisotropies by suppressing the growth of structure below the free-streaming scale. BAO are not sensitive to the latter effect at all, and only probe the background geometry by constraining the total matter density Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} and the parameter combination H0​rdH_{0}r_{\mathrm{d}}, so DESI BAO alone cannot constrain the neutrino masses. Nevertheless by breaking geometrical degeneracies, BAO significantly enhance the ability of the CMB to constrain this parameter.

The upper limits on ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} that we obtain from the combination of DESI and CMB depend on the particular choice of the CMB likelihood used, since the various likelihoods differ slightly in the amount of lensing power they infer from the lensed T​TTT, T​ETE and E​EEE power spectra. This can be incorporated into a phenomenological parameter ALA_{\rm L} that scales the model lensing power used to compute the lensed power spectra (but not the power reconstructed from the 4-point function), such that values AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 indicate an excess of lensing power, often referred to as the ‘ALA_{\rm L} anomaly’. Increasing ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} above 0.06 eV decreases the expected lensing power, while smaller values would boost it.

The baseline CMB likelihood we have adopted through this paper combines the CamSpec likelihood [108, 109] together with the combined CMB likelihood from Planck [166] and ACT [104], both of which are based on the PR4 data release. Combining these with the DESI DR2 BAO, and assuming a Λ\LambdaCDM background, we find the marginalized posterior limit

∑mν<0.064​eV(95%, DESI+CMB). \left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.064\,{\rm eV}\quad\text{(95\%,~DESI+CMB). }\right. (29)

Although the CamSpec likelihood appears to prefer a lower lensing power and reduces the ALA_{\rm L} anomaly [109], the tighter constraints on other cosmological parameters degenerate with ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} mean that this upper bound is tighter than the one obtained with the original Plik likelihood:

∑mν<0.069​eV(95%, DESI+CMB[Plik]). \left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.069\,{\rm eV}\quad\text{(95\%,~DESI+CMB[{Plik}]). }\right. (30)

The result of Eq. 30 is directly comparable to the result obtained from BAO and CMB in the DESI DR1 analysis [38, 46], which used the Plik likelihood as the default and obtained the corresponding constraint ∑mν<0.082\sum m_{\nu}<0.082 eV (95%).2121 21 Note that [38] originally reported a slightly tighter constraint due to a bug in the version of the ACT lensing likelihood used in that analysis. This was corrected in [46], where the quoted result was obtained using v1.2 of the ACT likelihood code that is also used here. This close to 20%20\% reduction in the upper bound reflects the higher precision of the DESI DR2 BAO data compared to DR1.

The use of the alternative LoLLiPoP and HiLLiPoP (L-H) likelihoods of [110] also show a lower excess lensing power than Plik. In this case, this effect is also reflected in significantly looser upper bounds on the neutrino mass,

∑mν<0.077​eV(95%, DESI+CMB[L-H]). \left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.077\,{\rm eV}\quad\text{(95\%,~DESI+CMB[{L-H}]). }\right. (31)

Figure 15 shows the marginalized 1D posterior constraints on ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} for the combination of DESI with each of the CMB likelihoods.

Irrespective of which CMB likelihood is used, all three upper bounds are very close to the lower bound ∑mν>0.059\sum m_{\nu}>0.059 eV set by neutrino oscillation experiments [167]. The posteriors shown in Figure 15 all resemble the tails of distributions that would peak at negative neutrino masses if this were allowed by the prior. This behavior has been explored in a few recent studies [161, 168, 163, 169], as well as in our companion work [50], which also shows that it holds for profile likelihoods based on extrapolating the χ2\chi^{2} likelihood surface to ∑mν<0\sum m_{\nu}<0 eV. In the context of a model with effective neutrino masses that are allowed to assume negative values, the DESI+CMB likelihood peaks at ∑mν,eff<0\sum m_{\nu,{\rm eff}}<0, and the tension with the minimal mass bound from terrestrial experiments increases to 3.0​σ3.0\sigma [50].

This discrepancy can be related to the tension between DESI and CMB results for the parameters Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} and H0​rdH_{0}r_{\mathrm{d}} in a Λ\LambdaCDM background discussed in Section VI above, and particularly in Figure 8. For fixed angular acoustic scale θ∗\theta_{\ast}, the effects on the CMB of changing ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} and changing Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} are positively correlated, as can be seen from the dashed black contour in Figure 16 (similar degeneracies can also be observed between ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} and H0​rdH_{0}r_{\mathrm{d}}, but with a negative correlation). In Λ\LambdaCDM, DESI tightly constrains Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}, as shown by the vertical shaded contour, to a value close to the low-end tail of the marginalized posterior distribution for CMB measurements. Consequently, the combination of DESI and CMB rules out all but the smallest neutrino masses. This result is thus related to the preference of DESI for lower values of Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} compared to the CMB discussed in the previous Sections.

As the upper limits on ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} from cosmology approach the lower limits from neutrino oscillations, the distinction between the different mass orderings becomes increasingly relevant. The baseline constraint Eq. 29, obtained assuming a ∑mν>0\sum m_{\nu}>0 prior, already appears to rule out the inverted ordering. However, to determine the evidence in support of the normal ordering, one should also account for the fact that much of the posterior volume violates the constraints for both mass orderings. To do this we use a physical model for the total mass ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} in terms of lightest neutrino mass ml≥0m_{l}\geq 0, which includes information on the mass squared splittings Δ​m212\Delta m_{21}^{2} and |Δ​m312||\Delta m_{31}^{2}| and allows for either mass ordering, as described in [170]. We then determine the upper bounds on this model from a combined analysis of DESI, CMB (with the baseline CamSpec likelihood) and 3-flavor oscillation constraints from NuFit-6.0 [167], assigning equal prior probabilities to either mass ordering. The result obtained is

∑mν<0.112​eV(95%, DESI+CMB+NuFit-6.0).\begin{split}\sum m_{\nu}<0.112\,{\rm eV}\quad\text{(95\%, DESI+CMB\allowbreak+}&\\ \text{NuFit-6.0)}.\end{split} (32)

The difference between the limits in Eq. 29 and Eq. 32 arises because the former only requires ∑mν>0\sum m_{\nu}>0 while the latter incorporates oscillation data that effectively require ∑mν>0.06​eV\sum m_{\nu}>0.06{\,\rm eV}, therefore pushing the upper limit into territory disfavored by the DESI+CMB data alone. In the supporting paper [50], we also compare the two mass orderings and find a Bayes factor of K=10K=10 providing strong evidence in support of the normal mass ordering under the assumption of the Λ\LambdaCDM+∑mν\sum m_{\nu} model.

Given the discrepancy between DESI and CMB under the Λ\LambdaCDM model, and the strong preference for a w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model discussed in Section VII, we consider the effect of allowing the equation-of-state parameters w0w_{0} and waw_{a} to vary. In this scenario and assuming a ∑mν>0\sum m_{\nu}>0 prior, we find

∑mν<0.163eV(95%, w0​waCDM: DESI+CMB),\begin{split}\sum m_{\nu}<0.163\,{\rm eV}\quad\text{(95\%, $w_{0}w_{a}$CDM: DESI+}&\\ \text{CMB),}\end{split} (33)

from combining DESI with CMB, and

∑mν<0.129eV(95%, w0​waCDM: DESI+CMB+DESY5)\begin{split}\sum m_{\nu}<0.129\,{\rm eV}\quad\text{(95\%, $w_{0}w_{a}$CDM: DESI+}&\\ \text{CMB+DESY5)}\end{split} (34)

when also using DESY5 SNe to better constrain the equation of state of dark energy. More details of parameter posteriors in this scenario, including those obtained with other data combinations and the wwCDM+∑mν\sum m_{\nu} model, are presented in Table 7. Through comparison to Table 5, we find that allowing ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} to vary with a conventional physical prior ∑mν>0\sum m_{\nu}>0 eV has little effect on the w⁡(z)w(z) constraints, but that allowing w0w_{0} and waw_{a} to vary significantly relaxes the neutrino mass bound in all cases. Moreover, in the case of DESI and CMB, the peak of the 1D marginalized posterior is recovered in the positive mass range, as shown in Figure 15.

In Λ\LambdaCDM, BAO measurements from DESI set a geometric constraint on Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} (or, equivalently, on H0​rdH_{0}r_{\mathrm{d}}) that helps break the degeneracy in the CMB results for ∑mν\sum m_{\nu}. In the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model, these geometric measurements primarily help by constraining the background w0w_{0} and waw_{a} values, thus limiting the available ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} range from the CMB alone, which is itself weaker than in Λ\LambdaCDM due to the additional freedom in the expansion history. This effect is even clearer when also adding SNe to DESI and CMB, as the constraints on the background become significantly tighter. This is illustrated in Figure 17, where the vertical blue bands show the purely geometrical constraints from DESI+DESY5. An extension of this plot where these degeneracies extend further in parameter space by allowing for negative neutrino masses through and effective parameter ∑mν,eff>0\sum m_{\nu,{\rm eff}}>0 is shown in [50].

Finally, constraints on the number of effective relativistic degrees of freedom, NeffN_{\mathrm{eff}}, are not discussed in detail here, but are consistent with the particle physics value Neff=3.044N_{\rm eff}=3.044 as described in our supporting paper [50].

IX Conclusions

We have presented BAO measurements from over 14 million discrete galaxy and quasar tracers drawn from the first three years of operation of DESI and which will be included in the second data release (DR2). These results use samples of nearby bright galaxies, LRGs, ELGs and quasars over the redshift range 0.1<z<2.10.1<z<2.1, and cover a cumulative effective volume of over 42​Gpc342\;{\rm Gpc}^{3}. Complementary BAO measurements from correlations of the Lyα\alpha forest and high-redshift quasars at effective redshift z=2.33z=2.33 are presented in the companion paper [63].

Our BAO analysis largely follows the methods used for the previous DESI DR1 analysis and presented in [21], but with improved statistical precision as the effective volume of the data has increased by more than a factor of two. Some particular differences include the use of a fainter limiting magnitude cut to define the bright galaxy sample, resulting in a higher number density, and the inclusion of quadrupole information in BAO fits to the quasar sample. As for the DR1 analysis, we applied a strict catalog-level blinding to our data while initial data checks were carried out and the analysis pipeline was being finalized. The validation tests and the criteria that were required to be met before the data were unblinded are described in detail in the supporting publication [48].

The final BAO results provide a precision on the isotropic distance scale measurement of DV/rdD_{\mathrm{V}}/r_{\mathrm{d}} that ranges from 1.54% (for the QSO) down to just 0.45% for our most constraining composite LRG3++ELG1 sample; other than for the QSO, the precision is sub-percent for every tracer and redshift range. We also obtained a precision of a few percent on the measurement of the Alcock-Paczyński distance ratio for every tracer except the lowest redshift BGS. Together these results are the most precise BAO measurements ever made at all redshifts covered, including at z<0.8z<0.8 where DESI DR2 now greatly exceeds the precision of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS).

The DR2 results are very consistent with those previously reported from the DR1 data that form a subset of DR2. The pp-value determined from the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for the distribution of the differences is 0.40. The DR2 results are also consistent with SDSS. [21] previously reported a ∼3​σ\sim 3\sigma discrepancy in the measurement of the transverse BAO scale DM/rdD_{\mathrm{M}}/r_{\mathrm{d}} in the LRG2 sample at effective redshift zeff=0.706z_{\rm eff}=0.706 compared to the equivalent result from SDSS. For DR2, the difference has decreased in significance, lying within the range 1.5​σ1.5\sigma to 2.6​σ2.6\sigma, depending on assumptions about the degree of correlation between the two samples.

The combination of all BAO measurements from DR2 is well fit by a flat Λ\LambdaCDM cosmological model with matter density parameter Ωm=0.2975±0.0086\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}=0.2975\pm 0.0086 and product of the scaled Hubble constant and sound horizon at the drag epoch h​rd=(101.54±0.73)hr_{\mathrm{d}}=(101.54\pm 0.73) Mpc. This represents a 40% improvement in precision compared to the equivalent results from DR1, but with excellent consistency between the two. However, while a Λ\LambdaCDM model provides a good fit to DESI data, the model parameters obtained from this fit are now in 2.3σ\sigma tension with those derived from the CMB, increased from 1.9σ\sigma in DR1. This tension is present despite DESI being consistent with the acoustic angular scale θ∗\theta_{*} measured by CMB.

When calibrated with an external prior on Ωb​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{b}}h^{2} from BBN, our BAO measurements correspond to a value H0=(68.50±0.58)​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=(68.50\pm 0.58)\;\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} in Λ\LambdaCDM, a value that is independent of any information on CMB anisotropies. In the Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}-H0H_{0} plane, the results from BBN-calibrated BAO are now more discrepant with those from CMB; the offset of the results is again along the Ωm​h3=constant\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{3}={\rm constant} degeneracy direction of the CMB that is determined by the very precisely measured acoustic angular scale θ∗\theta_{\ast}. Combining DESI BAO with BBN and the Planck θ∗\theta_{\ast} result gives H0=(68.45±0.47)​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=(68.45\pm 0.47)\;\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}, a 0.7% precision measurement competitive with that from the CMB itself, and in strong disagreement with SH0ES [129].

Within the Λ\LambdaCDM framework, DESI results are also somewhat in tension with the high Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} values preferred by SNe datasets, which—contrary to DESI—prefer larger Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} than Planck. While not individually rising to the 3​σ3\sigma significance threshold, these results point to an incompatibility between different cosmological datasets when interpreted in the Λ\LambdaCDM model. Interestingly, the relative levels of Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} and H0H_{0} values currently measured by SN, DESI and CMB datasets match what would be expected if data from a true evolving dark energy model were analyzed in the restrictive Λ\LambdaCDM model, as pointed out recently by [131].

Assuming a Λ\LambdaCDM background, the combination of DESI and CMB data give the tightest upper bound on the neutrino mass sum to date, ∑mν<0.064\sum m_{\nu}<0.064 eV (95% limit) in our baseline analysis. Although this relaxes to ∑mν<0.078\sum m_{\nu}<0.078 eV when using an alternative Planck likelihood [110], both results are approaching the lower bound set by terrestrial neutrino oscillation experiments, ∑mν≥0.059\sum m_{\nu}\geq 0.059 eV. Indeed, if the model is extended to allow for negative ‘effective’ neutrino masses, most of the posterior mass and the peak of the likelihood lie at ∑mν,eff<0\sum m_{\nu,{\rm eff}}<0 eV, another possible sign of growing tensions within the Λ\LambdaCDM model with DESI DR2 [50].

The evidence for a departure from Λ\LambdaCDM in the form of evolving dark energy has increased with the DR2 BAO data. Comparing the evolving dark energy model parametrized by w⁡(a)=w0+wa​(1−a)w(a)=w_{0}+w_{a}(1-a) to Λ\LambdaCDM, we find a 3.1​σ3.1\sigma evidence in favor of dynamical dark energy from DESI+CMB alone. When we add the recent Pantheon+, Union3 or DESY5 SNe datasets to this combination, the preference for w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM over Λ\LambdaCDM is 2.8​σ2.8\sigma, 3.8​σ3.8\sigma or 4.2​σ4.2\sigma respectively, with all three giving results for w0w_{0} and waw_{a} consistent with each other within their 68% credible regions. The preferences for w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM under these dataset combinations have increased compared to our DR1 results in [38]. All combinations of available datasets we study favor mutually consistent results with w0>−1w_{0}>-1 and wa<0w_{a}<0, apparently indicating a weakening dark energy today and a phantom crossing at some point in the past (in this parametrization). The supporting paper [49] examines this behavior using a wider range of models and non-parametric methods. We note that the degeneracy direction for the constraints in the w0w_{0}-waw_{a} plane approximately points towards the Λ\LambdaCDM solution, although this is neither exact nor consistent between fits to different combinations of datasets. This constitutes a weak coincidence as there is no a priori reason for the best-fit values of w0w_{0} and waw_{a} to have the values that lead to this observation.

In Sections VII.2 and VII.3, we examined the contributions to the preference for evolving dark energy in detail. For DESI+CMB, the discrepancy in preferred Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} values in Λ\LambdaCDM is resolved in w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM, leading to the 3.1​σ3.1\sigma (Δ​χMAP2=−12.5\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=-12.5) preference for the latter. If we omit CMB lensing the best-fit w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM parameters are unchanged, though the significance drops to 2.7​σ2.7\sigma (Δ​χMAP2=−9.7\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=-9.7). If we also marginalize over any late-time dependence in the CMB and only impose a prior on (θ∗,ωb,ωbc)(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}}), there is a further slight reduction to 2.4​σ2.4\sigma (Δ​χMAP2=−8.0\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}}=-8.0). The w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM and ‘compromise’ Λ\LambdaCDM models predict different evolution of the distance-redshift relation at z<0.4z<0.4, with a ∼2%\sim 2\% difference in distances at z<0.1z<0.1. BAO do not provide high precision in this regime, but supernovae do, and the DESY5 and Union3 samples clearly favor the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM prediction. However, the distance-redshift evolution in the Pantheon+ analysis is closer to the Λ\LambdaCDM prediction, so adding Pantheon+ to DESI+CMB does not strengthen the evidence for w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM. Appendix A shows that our results are robust to changes in the choice of CMB likelihood. We also show that replacing the CMB likelihood with the weak gravitational lensing constraints from the DESY3 (3×\times2pt) analysis retains a clear preference for evolving dark energy, with, e.g., a ≳3​σ\gtrsim 3\sigma preference for w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM from DESI+DESY3 (3×\times2pt)+DESY5 SNe. Removing the preference for w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM through changes to the DESI measurements themselves would require systematic errors to be far larger than any found in our tests.

In the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM background model, when the neutrino mass scale is allowed to vary with physical non-negative prior bounds, the upper limit on ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} is significantly relaxed to ∑mν<0.16\sum m_{\nu}<0.16 eV (95%, from DESI+CMB) or ∑mν<0.13\sum m_{\nu}<0.13 eV (95%, from DESI+CMB+DESY5, the middle result from the three possible SNe samples), while the constraints on w0w_{0} and waw_{a} do not materially change from the case where ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} is fixed. These limits are entirely consistent with neutrino oscillation experiment results. The supporting paper [50] shows that even when allowing for effective masses ∑mν,eff\sum m_{\nu,{\rm eff}} with a wide prior that allows negative values, the marginalized posterior in w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM from DESI+CMB is consistent with the oscillation lower limit and its peak lies in the positive region.

In [38] we characterized the results from DESI DR1 and external datasets as providing “a tantalizing suggestion of deviations from the standard cosmological model”. The DR2 data presented here have sharpened this evidence, although significance levels still vary depending on the external data used—particularly the choice of SNe sample—and no combination exceeds 4.2​σ4.2\sigma. Nevertheless, it is becoming clear that unless some unidentified systematic error affects one or several of the different cosmological datasets used, the challenge to the Λ\LambdaCDM model has increased. Sharper measurements from future DESI analyses and from other experiments will show whether these challenges to the standard cosmological model herald yet another radical transformation in our understanding of the evolution and energy content of the Universe.

X Data Availability

The data used in this analysis will be made public along with Data Release 2 (details in https://data.desi.lbl.gov/doc/releases/). BAO likelihoods for DESI DR2, integrated in the cobaya code, are available at https://github.com/CobayaSampler/bao_data. The data points corresponding to the figures from this paper are available in Ref. [171].

Appendix A Early-Universe priors and robustness to choice of CMB likelihoods

As discussed in Section IV, for some purposes it is convenient to make use of a compression of the full CMB information into a multivariate correlated Gaussian prior on the quantities θ∗\theta_{\ast}, ωbc\omega_{\mathrm{bc}} and ωb\omega_{\mathrm{b}}, which are early-Universe quantities that can be determined independently of assumptions about the late-time evolution by maginalizing over late-time effects such as the ISW effect and CMB lensing. This process was performed by [111] based on the CamSpec CMB likelihood. We use their results to define a Gaussian prior with mean

𝝁⁡(θ∗,ωb,ωbc)=(0.010410.022230.14208)\bm{\mu}(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}})=\begin{pmatrix}0.01041\\ 0.02223\\ 0.14208\end{pmatrix} (35)

and covariance

𝐂=10−9×(0.0066210.12444−1.19290.1244421.344−94.001−1.1929−94.0011488.4).\mathbf{C}=10^{-9}\times\begin{pmatrix}0.006621&0.12444&-1.1929\\ 0.12444&21.344&-94.001\\ -1.1929&-94.001&1488.4\end{pmatrix}\,. (36)

The use of this prior has been indicated throughout the paper by the use of the (θ∗,ωb,ωbc)CMB(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}})_{\rm CMB} notation. As shown in the left panel of Figure 14 the posterior results for the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM model are remarkably similar in all cases when comparing fits to DESI+(θ∗,ωb,ωbc)CMB(\theta_{\ast},\omega_{\mathrm{b}},\omega_{\mathrm{bc}})_{\rm CMB}, DESI+CMB (with full CMB information) and DESI+CMB (no lensing), indicating that most of the information added by the CMB in this scenario comes from the anchoring constraint it provides on Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}, limiting the freedom of the model to absorb background expansion effects of w0w_{0} and waw_{a} into other parameters. We also tested a separate compression of the CMB information based on the shift parameters RR and lAl_{A} together with ωb\omega_{\mathrm{b}} [112] and found that it gave very consistent results as well (see also [172]). Nevertheless, while the addition of CMB lensing information does not noticeably shift the w0w_{0}-waw_{a} posteriors, it does appreciably change the Δ​χMAP2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{MAP}} values and thus the significance of rejection of Λ\LambdaCDM.

Figure 18 shows the differences in the constraints obtained from the DESI+CMB+DESY5 data combination in the w0​waw_{0}w_{a}CDM case, arising from the use of the three different CMB likelihoods, namely CamSpec (our baseline in this paper), Plik and L-H (cf. Section IV for descriptions). The results using CamSpec and Plik are remarkably consistent, though we see a small shift at the 0.1​σ0.1\sigma level when using L-H PR4.

Appendix B Robustness to assumption about correlation in BAO systematic errors

Our baseline approach, described briefly in Section III and in more detail in [48], assumes that the systematic error contributions to BAO measurements are not correlated with each other across redshift bins. As a robustness test, we evaluated the impact of introducing off-diagonal terms in the systematics covariance matrix of the BAO measurements. To do this, we assumed that the theoretical modelling systematic error contributions, which are estimated to be 0.1% in αiso\alpha_{\mathrm{iso}} and 0.2% in αAP\alpha_{\rm AP}, are correlated across all redshift bins, with a correlation coefficient of 0.5. This leads to redshift-dependent correlations in the final covariance matrix. We found that including these correlations had no detectable effect on the cosmological constraints obtained in any model or combination of DESI with any external dataset. This result is unsurprising, since the systematic errors are subdominant to statistical errors in all redshift bins, so correlations in the systematic errors cannot play a large role.
